I picked up this game because I really enjoyed Dark Souls 1, 2, and 3, as well as Elden Ring. Sekiro plays quite differently in several ways. The focus on experience and Sen (currency) feels very different from the Souls games, and the skill progression system replaces the heavy emphasis on weapon movesets with something entirely its own.

That said, the core elements I love about FromSoftware games are still here: challenging combat, rewarding exploration, and the satisfaction of overcoming difficult encounters through persistence. Those are the aspects I enjoyed most in the Souls series, and they're what I'm enjoying most about Sekiro as well.

So far, I've found the different approach to character progression both interesting and enjoyable. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes other FromSoftware titles, but it's worth knowing going in that it has a distinct feel and isn't simply another Dark Souls.

All the worst aspects of the form soft souls games without the good parts, i guess play it if you are good with parrying but avoid if you're not, some of the most frustarating boss runbacks, unenjoyable stealth and oddly punishing for dying in a game where a lot of enemies take off almost half of your health in one hit

citations.review_text: Shinobi Rhythm Game, peak af

An amazing game with the best souls combat there is. It's a rhythm game in disguise.

Stuttered a bit on PC but was amazing on steam deck.

Sekiro is indisputably the best game FromSoftware has ever created in terms of mechanical combat. It delivers a hyper addictive gameplay loop that demands absolute, unadulterated skill. While many label it the hardest entry in the "Soulsborne" pantheon, it is also easily the most deeply rewarding to master.


The genius of Sekiro lies in its Posture System, which is vastly deeper, more intelligent, and frankly way less goofy looking than standard action games. In typical Souls games, your primary defense is the panic roll you spend half the boss fight repeatedly tumbling across the floor like an acrobat just to escape a hit.

Sekiro eliminates that entirely. You don't run, and you don't roll. You stand your ground, look a ten-foot-tall boss dead in the eye, and meet their blade face-to-face. Because perfect deflections deal posture damage, defense becomes an offensive mechanic. Every parry is a statement. It transforms the combat into a beautiful, high-stakes dance of clashing steel where you feel like an absolute anime legend slashing, hacking, and controlling the rhythm of the blade.


The narrative and setting get a massive plus. Unlike other FromSoft titles, the lore isn’t buried in cryptic item descriptions you don't need to read the underwear of a zombie soldier just to understand the plot. Sekiro delivers a clear, compelling, and emotionally driven story from start to finish. Because the narrative actually moves forward, the New Game Plus (NG+) cycles stay fast and aggressive, never letting the momentum run dull.


9/10 strongly recommends

My only regret is waiting till 2026 to play this masterpiece.

The game is very hard early on when you still don't know the basics, so prepare to die a lot until you learn how to play. Whoever treats it as an action game will suffer and get frustrated.

While it's a FromSoftware game, it feels different from the other titles, doesn't play the same, and only shares a few mechanics with the Souls games.

Graphics are still good in 2026, with very nice scenery, and while it's kind of an open world, it's small enough that it doesn't even have a map.

Bosses and mini bosses are well crafted, each one challenges you to apply what you learned, and some bosses act like a skill check, you shall not pass until you learn how to play this game. Most importantly, there is no difficulty setting, the only way forward is to get good, and once you do, you'll appreciate the time spent mastering your skills. In the end, you'll reach a level where the fights feel like a rhythm game. Easily one of the best combat systems in gaming and among the very best when it comes to parrying.

I was never this satisfied after beating a boss in a game. Highly recommended for anyone patient enough to learn instead of just button mashing, this game is as memorable as it gets.

Absolute Cinema!

Flawless combat system for those who love a balance of deflection mechanics, rhythm-based gameplay, and prosthetic tools.

Great bosses and beautifully interconnected game areas.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game lacks a traditional leveling or stat-grinding system, meaning player progression relies on mastering mechanics and defeating major bosses for memories that increase attack power.

citations.review_text:
68 Hours | 100% Achievements | Full Completion

I have 68 hours in Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice and have earned 100% of the achievements, so I've experienced everything the game has to offer. As someone who's beaten Demon's Souls (PS5), Dark Souls, Dark Souls III, and Elden Ring, I'd consider myself fairly experienced with FromSoftware games. Here's what I thought:

• Yes, the game is difficult. However, the resurrection mechanic makes death a little less punishing than it first seems, since you often get a second chance during a fight.

• There's no traditional leveling system. Instead, every major boss drops a Memory that permanently increases your Attack Power. It keeps progression simple while still making every major victory feel rewarding.

• The progression is fantastic. You unlock Prosthetic Tools that completely change combat, such as throwing shurikens, using fire, or deploying an umbrella to block attacks. They add a lot of variety without taking away from the swordplay.

• Skill trees give meaningful upgrades. Defeating enemies earns experience, and every level gives you a skill point to spend on new combat techniques, passive abilities, and weapon arts. Unlocking new skills always felt rewarding.

• The combat is incredible. Deflecting attacks, breaking enemy posture, and learning each boss's rhythm creates some of the most satisfying combat I've ever played.

• The story is very good. It's engaging and memorable, although I wouldn't call it perfect.

• The graphics have aged well. Even though the game is over seven years old, it still looks fantastic thanks to its art direction.

• The movement is amazing. The parkour, wall jumping, and grappling hook make exploration fast, fluid, and incredibly fun.

Overall: Sekiro is one of the best action games I've ever played. If you're looking for a challenging but incredibly rewarding experience, I can't recommend it enough.

Sekiro is easily my favorite Soulslike.
I have countless runs on console, but it just never gets boring.

There's no builds, there's no armors, no stats to grind. It's just you, the one-armed wolf, with your sword -- and learning the game. Raw
It's more focused and that's why it works so well.
Every fight is purely a skill check, there's no gear or numbers to help make it easy.

You fight, and you die. And you fight again. No "hold up, let me grind a bit to get a bit of an extra edge".

Combat is just perfect. It's a mix between offense and defense, with the most beautiful deflect system I've ever seen in games. It's a rhythm game where you don't run away or roll away from your enemies... you stand your ground, clash blade against blade and wait for your opening to strike.
Every boss you defeat feels earned in a way that few games can.

The setting is also a huge plus. Feudal japan but with a grim setting, a grey, dim world with dark fanstasy stuff.
The world feels so beautiful in its melancholic vibes.

It's hard, but never unfair. You learn patters, you learn to keep calm and not panic, you improve, and you realize that there's no such thing as unfair in this game.

An absolute masterpiece.

I'm speechless with this game... What a ride it was, i loved it throughout the whole journey.. This feels really different to other fromsoft games because you don't grow stats or anything like that, but the feeling of learning the fight, parrying your way into submission, is unmatched! i love the utter aggression that the game incentivizes you to go for.. And i loved the setting, feudal Japan with magic and lore im a sucker for these.. And this game is gorgeous, wonderfully voiced in japanese, with crazy art design.. I see how it won goty back in 2019.. Im really happy i got to experience this masterpiece! Thank you fromsoftware!

- Final boss feels like a final boss, very tough fight even tough for me he was 2nd hardest.
- Story was mid but it was there and understadable, I knew what to do since the NPC told me and I did not have to guess only to figure out how to reach places.

The Bad:

- This is not Sekiro specific but all soul games suffer from this, can I get a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ quest journal just to know what is my next target, you dont need to tell me where to go but just a little note.
- Side quests do not exist ( Yes you can explore and do random bosses which you dont have to fight but that is exploration ).
- Too punishing for dying, I perosnally got a mod to fix that but I think it was -70% money. You die a lot so it felt an uncessary obstacle in a soul game even when money is used later on mostly.

I highly recommend this game but the price tag is kinda meh, try to get it on sale obviously.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the PC version is capped at 60 FPS and locked to a 16:9 aspect ratio by default, requiring mods to fix.

citations.review_text:
It's a beautiful game of high highs and low lows. Unfortunately I think the lows are too low for me.

I love the foundational combat. I want to just R1 and parry all day. I'll tolerate jumping and dodging. But unfortunately there's more.

I found myself wishing the tool system and consumables weren't even in the game. They enable gimmicky fights designed around them, which are prohibitively difficult and annoying if you don't want to engage with those systems. Both depend on scarce resources. If there's a limited amount of something, it means I'm never using it; might as well not be there.

I was also routinely peeved by dangerous thrusts and sweeps having the same symbol. Why have that piece of visual language at all if the response to one gets you punished by the other? At that point just don't have a distracting symbol/sound at all and let me focus on the animation to decide what to do.

Lastly: dragonrot. Just why? I already got punished for dying by losing time, money, and xp, but now I lose access to quests and some NPCs too? I don't see how repeated attempts at learning a fight should be something the game systemically discourages.

Oh, I almost forgot. Stock, it's FPS capped at 60 and locked at 16:9. Thankfully, both of these can be fixed with mods.

Glazers will never admit this game isn't perfect, so I'm sorry to break the news.

Can't believe Miyazaki whipped up peak experience just to tide us over until Elden Ring. I kinda gave up on this game to play souls/Bloodborne but I decided to start over and play it again, and I ended up platting it. Here's REAL tips on how to win:

-Use a guide (I recommend a checklist), if at least on your second playthrough. There is simply no way to figure out how to get all endings and complete all side quests on your own
-Use the Sekiro FPS unlocker
-If you want to plat/get all gauntlets, at minimum you'll need to do a 100% run, then do a 90% run (up to main fountainhead boss) on NG+, and then save scum to go back and side with Kuro to get the bosses trophy and unlock the Shura gauntlet (must be on the same save file).

Pros:

-Best sound design of any soul game
-Best bosses of any souls game (besides ER probably)
-Best combat of any game ever (you can be as simple or flashy as you want)
-Level/world design might genuinely be second to DS1
-The story/lore is simpler with less lore than its FS brothers, but genius nonetheless


Cons:
-Headless
-XP farming (NG+ is pretty generous tho)
-the game ended :(

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat system as heavily focused on parrying, deflecting, and rhythm rather than traditional role-playing game mechanics.

citations.review_text: Similar to Elden Ring, but different fighting style that emphasizes parrying

Sekiro is for those of us who don't want to do a new build with a new weapon every time, who don't need slight stat variations or a different weapon animation to keep the game fun. It's about the combat, the patterns, the timing, and the subtle decision-making, and Sekiro has those mastered. The posture and parry systems provide and intensity that keeps most encounters locked to a tight pace rather than having too many long pauses to run around. Yet there's still plenty of value in pushing yourself to use all of the damage avoidance mechanics rather than fall into a one-dimensional rhythm.

Oddly, the bosses in Sekiro don't stand out to me as much as those from the Souls series, but I think that's because the bar is so high, and the focus is as much on mastering the overall system as it is on each individual boss's quirks. The highs are not just towering, but are consistent.

It's basically rythm game that make you dance your way to victory, clashing sword, and occasional dodge. 100% recommended for anyone that love challenging game. My first ever Formsoftware tittle that i finished followed with elden ring and lies of P. 

The memory features give you opportunity to rematch with any boss you already defeated should you want to master them or trying some combos and trick.

Worth every single penny, but with  the age, just wait for $40 bucks discount, i doubt they will get lower than that

This game is kinda like both Miyazakis got together and made a game and I cannot say enough good things about it.  Its beautiful, intense, very challenging and full of memorable moments.  Unlike other titles from FromSoftware, the story is told in a much clearer manner, with the protagonist, Wolf, even speaking quite a bit! Its also full of wonderful (even if they are quite sad sometimes) moments between the characters making some of them easy to connect with and even fall in love with. The boss battles are also what we've come to expect from FromSoftware, as well but more challenging due to the fact that it does not follow the typical Souls combat formula.  Part of the challenge is adapting your playstyle - Its'd definitely not a 1:1 with the usual Souls formula and there's a lot to be unlearned.  Its been said in a lot of the reviews - the playstyle is VERY aggressive and rewards aggressive play moreso than any of their other titles.  I'd also go so far as to say its not a Soulslike, but more of a very difficult rhythm game.
best rhythm game ong also isshin got his grippers out 😋😋😋👅👅👅👅👅

This game has the greatest combat of any game I've ever played, and it's not even close.

MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD

This is my second Fromsoftware game after playing Dark Souls 1. I absolutely loved Dark Souls and happened to have Sekiro collecting dust in my library so I picked it back up again. The first time I played it a few years ago I got up to the second general in the Ashina Outskirts and got busy and gave up. I felt punished and scared by the Dragonrot mechanic so much so that it shooed me away from ever going deeper into the game. After dying countless times in Dark Souls and learning what it means to not go hollow, I found an absolute masterpiece. 

However, my experience didn't begin with many positive opinions. My first impressions were that all of the habits I picked up from Dark Souls were punishing me into the ground. My mindset was stuck always trying to watch the opponent and react to their moves; to never attack first. Over time, I started to get a better understanding of the style and rhythm of combat, and it started to become more like a dance. The biggest standout moment to me was my fight against Lady Butterfly. She'll hit you will a flurry of attacks and I just kept losing. Until I figured out how to parry her. My god, I'm not sure if anything is quite as satisfying as parrying all of a boss's combo. I entered such a flow state in that fight I was practically high when I beat her. At that exact moment, I realized that this game is one of the greatest I've ever had the pleasure of touching. 

Everything after that is superb. Almost all of the boss fights are excellent, with the exception of some stinkers that really don't feel like they fit in the game at first. But even the ones that I hated initially, I started to grow fonder and fonder throughout my next playthroughs. I now appriciate that those bosses that initially felt they didn't belong, allowed me to learn a larger array of skill expression in the combat system.

Before I begin, this down vote is not due to skill issue. I literally killed all bosses multiple times and the only time I used the shinobi umbrella was during inner ishin. And no I havent touched modded sekiro yet but I plan to in the near future.

But from software has this thing where it blurs the lines between difficult and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tedious. For example it tells you that certain unblockable attacks can be jumped over simple enough. What it doesnt tell you is that certain attacks that definitely look like they'd ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ one shot you if you jumped you just get invulnerablility frames. The worst example is the demon of hatred's perilous attack like he literally phases through your body and if you've played older games especially metroid vania ones then you'll know that touching an enemy with your pinky toe means you take full damage.

The only way you would know about these invulnerable frames is if you allowed yourself to get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annihilated and just happened to realize you had iframes. Spirit emblem system is mediocre, you only have a limited amount so it discourages using those super cool hard hitting attacks because it shares resources with tools that allow you to cheese the game like the fire crackers. If you perfectly parry an perilous attack or perform a mikiri counter you should be able to regenerate a few spirit emblems to encourage using all the tools you have. Another example of this is lightning reversal. Basically how it works is if you take lightning damage while in the air you can counter it back at the enemy if you perform the counter before landing. This works with other combat arts that jump your character into the air.
